value: Few studies have compared patient and physician attitudes regarding placebo interventions in medical practice. This study surveyed 414 primary care patients and 232 general practitioners in Zurich, Switzerland, to compare their perspectives on therapies working through self-healing or contextual factors. While both groups largely believed in the effectiveness of therapy belief (87% patients, 97% GPs), patients generally showed more support for non-specific interventions than physicians, despite 90% of GPs admitting to actively using such effects. Crucially, 70% of patients desired explicit information when receiving non-specific interventions, a preference GPs significantly underestimated (estimating 33%). Patients also expressed greater disappointment when unknowingly treated with pure placebos (e.g., sugar pills) than impure ones (e.g., herbal remedies). The findings suggest that physicians underestimate patient openness to non-specific therapies, emphasizing the need for professional standards to ethically integrate placebo effects while maintaining authenticity and credibility, as patients desire transparency.
